column11: Lu M, Zhou Y, Haller IV et al., 'Increasing Prevalence of Primary Biliary Cholangitis and Reduced Mortality With Treatment', Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2018;16(8):1342-1350.e1 (doi 10.1016/j.cgh.2017.12.033, PMID 29277621), the Fibrotic Liver Disease Consortium, 3,488 patients across 11 US health systems 2003 to 2014: 'From 2006 through 2014, the prevalence of PBC increased from 21.7 to 39.2 per 100,000 persons.' 39.2 per 100,000 applied to the 318,301,008 US residents at 1 July 2014 (Census Bureau Vintage 2019, nst-est2019-alldata.csv) = 124,774. column12: THE YEAR IS 2014 AND IT IS NOT ROLLED FORWARD. The same paper has prevalence rising 3.0% to 7.5% a year by age group, so a 2026 figure would be materially higher, but no free source publishes a current-year US PBC prevalence and extrapolating the trend would be an estimate rather than a citation. The row therefore reads low. The companion FOLD paper (Lu M, Li J, Haller IV et al., Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2018;16(8):1333-1341.e6, doi 10.1016/j.cgh.2017.10.018, PMID 29066370) gives a 12-year period prevalence of 29.3 per 100,000 from 4,241 cases in 14.5 million patients, a different construct; the 39.2 point estimate is the right anchor

column12: TWO THINGS PULL IT OPPOSITE WAYS AND NEITHER IS APPLIED. (a) It reads LOW because the label also covers UDCA intolerance as monotherapy, and the same paper reports 'the overall rate of UDCA discontinuation was 12%'; that is not added because the paper gives no joint figure and the two groups can overlap. (b) It reads LOW again because only part of the population is ever assessed: the same paper finds just 52% received appropriate alkaline phosphatase testing at about a year, so measured inadequate response is itself an undercount. (c) Against both, the widely quoted '30% to 40% inadequate response' is EUROPEAN - Paris I/II criteria in tertiary referral cohorts - and should not be substituted for a US routine-care measurement; at 35% this pool would be 43,671 rather than 23,707, nearly double

column11: ALL OF IT, AND THIS IS THE ANSWER. The queue says 'the label does not cover this indication'. It does. MeSH D008105, 'Liver Cirrhosis, Biliary', IS primary biliary cholangitis, the disease formerly called primary biliary cirrhosis, and the label reads 'LIVDELZI is indicated for the treatment of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) in combination with ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) in adults who have had an inadequate response to UDCA, or as monotherapy in patients unable to tolerate UDCA' (DailyMed setid 89f79d98-135c-40b2-a585-6996c04e599c, SPL version 3, effective 2026-02-10, the Livdelzi row in the book's labels table; NDA 217899 approved 2024-08-14, the book's approvals table). The study is in that same approved population: NCT03301506 is 'Study of Seladelpar in Participants With Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)', Phase 3, 340 enrolled, ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING, whose primary outcome is 'Treatment emergent adverse events (TEAEs) ... biochemistry and hematology results' - the open-label long-term safety extension, and the book's own trials table records its condition as 'Primary Biliary Cirrhosis'
column12: ONE THING A HUMAN SHOULD NOT MISREAD. Livdelzi holds an ACCELERATED approval: 'This indication is approved under accelerated approval based on a reduction of alkaline phosphatase (ALP). Improvement in survival or prevention of liver decompensation events have not been demonstrated. Continued approval for this indication may be contingent upon verification and description of clinical benefit in confirmatory trial(s).' That is real risk, but it is DOWNSIDE ON THE EXISTING BASE, not an unpriced expansion layer, and it does not belong in an indication layer. It is also not this study: a safety extension with a TEAE primary endpoint is not the confirmatory outcomes trial. 1.0 is a final answer and the layer should be closed, not built
